comment:
Normative cross-language conformance vectors for apple-purchase-receipt-verifier.
One case per semantic fact: java/, node/, python/, swift/, go/, ruby/, rust/, php/ and dotnet/
each assert many of these under their own test names, and the duplicates are merged here.
Every expectation in this file was derived by hand from the four test-suite inventories,
from PLAN.md sections 2.1-2.3, from COMPARISON.md and from the fixture generator
(java/src/test/.../FixtureGeneratorTest.java) plus fixtures/generated/manifest.json.
NOTHING here was produced by running an implementation and recording what it did:
a vector that disagrees with an implementation is a bug report against that implementation
until a human decides otherwise.

Paths in "fields" are language-neutral. Scalars use the shared API names from PLAN.md section 3
(camelCase) for verifyTransaction/verifyAppTransaction/verifyRaw/verifyReceipt, and the literal
Apple wire keys (snake_case) for verifyReceiptEndpoint. "x.length" is a collection size.
"list[key=value].field" selects the single element of list whose key equals value.
"unknownAttributes[9999][0]" indexes the raw values recorded for receipt attribute type 9999,
expressed as a lowercase hex string. Dates are ISO-8601 UTC strings; claims that Apple ships as
epoch milliseconds (signedDate, receiptCreationDate) stay numbers. null means "absent or unset".
A field a case does not list is simply not pinned by that case.

Certificate-validity windows are judged at the payload signedDate / receipt creationDate, and
where the input states neither, at the SYSTEM clock — never at an injected one (PLAN.md 2.1
step 4, 2.2 step 2). The expired-chain cases are therefore deterministic. "clock" appears where
the answer genuinely moves with time — the max-signed-age staleness rule and the request_date
triple of the verifyReceipt endpoint — and, on the four dateless inputs, precisely to pin that
the answer does NOT move: a receipt or payload carrying no date of its own, verified under a
clock planted inside an expired certificate's window or far past a live one's, must reach the
verdict it reaches on real time. A caller injecting a clock to test staleness, or to work
around clock skew, must not thereby accept a chain that is expired. verifyReceipt cases cannot
carry a clock at all — the schema refuses one — because ReceiptVerifier takes no clock
parameter in any port. Where the schema does allow one, a runner MUST hand the case's clock to
the verifier rather than fake time; a case carrying a clock that is run against the system
clock is not running the case.

Every fixture records the SHA-256 of its DECODED logical bytes (post-codec: the file bytes for
raw, the base64-decoded bytes for base64, the trimmed UTF-8 for utf8). contentSha256 is not
documentation: tools/lint-cases.mjs re-hashes every registered fixture, and so does every
adapter — over the whole registry before any case runs, and again for each fixture a case
loads. A fixture that is regenerated, re-encoded or quietly edited fails loudly in every
language instead of silently changing what these vectors mean.

Four places where the ports had drifted apart were adjudicated and are pinned here: the
certificate-validity fallback clock (the dateless cases), the typed endpoint environment
(config.environment is the enum, and both values are exercised), and a receipt attribute type
above 2^31-1, which every port must reject as INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT rather than rename or
clamp. The fourth — verifyReceiptCore being public in every port, so no endpoint has to build a
wildcard-bundle-id verifier to reach it — changes no observable answer, so no vector can hold
it; the native suites carry that one.

"fault" names the one intentional defect of a negative case. It is documentation, not an
assertion: implementations are not required to report it, only to report the given reason.

Receipt base64 (added 2026-09-04). Every runner decodes a base64 fixture itself and hands DER to the library, so no verifyReceipt case can say how a port treats the string a client actually sent. The text codec and the verifyReceiptBase64 operation close that: the fixture bytes go to the string entry point verbatim, and a verifyReceiptEndpoint case over a text fixture puts them in receipt-data verbatim. The rule they pin is Apple's: receipt-data is Base64 as defined in RFC 4648, and Foundation's base64EncodedString(options:) can emit the standard or the base64url alphabet, with or without padding, with CR/LF line endings at 64 or 76 columns. Everything Foundation can emit is accepted; a character outside both alphabets, a mixed alphabet, anything after the padding (a third '=' included), a partial padding run, and an empty string are INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT (21002 at the endpoint). Padding is accepted omitted or canonical, never over- or under-supplied: no encoder emits either, and a decoder that recomputes it turns padding into a free suffix.

Hostile JWS (added 2026-09-05). Six inputs that Python's coverage-guided fuzzing walked out of the library as bare exceptions rather than verdicts are pinned here, so that all nine ports answer them and answer them the same way. A seventh input sits with them carrying no defect at all: the same signedDate spelled 1722945600000.0, which must verify, because a port could otherwise pass the out-of-range vector by refusing every number that is not a bare integer. Each is a real JWS over the generated test PKI carrying exactly one mutation; the header is signed in its hostile state so the ES256 signature covers the bytes served, and a mutated certificate is re-signed by its issuer so a broken issuer signature can never be the first thing a port objects to. The reasons were adjudicated against Node and Python, which already agreed on three of the five, and on the fourth the majority was overruled for the reason that case states: x5c entries that are not strings are INVALID_JWS_FORMAT, a signedDate of 1e300 is INVALID_CHAIN, a certificate that stops decoding inside its extension block is INVALID_CERTIFICATE, an unimplemented EC curve on the intermediate is INVALID_CERTIFICATE, and a certificate claiming X.509 version 11 is INVALID_CERTIFICATE, and a certificate carrying the same extension twice is INVALID_CERTIFICATE. The per-case descriptions carry the reasoning for each. What these five have in common is where the defect sits: in the JWS header and in the x5c certificates, both of which every port decodes BEFORE the signature that would have rejected them, and neither of which any signature in the input authenticates. An eighth input joined them when the x5c[2] differential was closed: the third x5c entry holding base64 of "not a certificate", which java alone rejected because java alone parsed that entry. The other eight ports verified the JWS, and the majority lost to the same rule the unimplemented curve lost to — pinning acceptance would have made java drop a rejection it already makes. Every port now parses all three entries; none of them trusts the third, which is what the differential was always about.

Receipt signer certificates (added 2026-09-05). The four certificate mutations above sit in a JWS header, and four ports answered them from checks written on the JWS path alone (node, python, ruby and dotnet; rust and php had them in a shared certificate parser, and java, swift and go get them from a platform decoder). So the same four mutations — X.509 version 11, a duplicated basicConstraints, an unassigned EC curve and an extension block that stops decoding — are built into the certificate a legacy PKCS#7 receipt is signed by, and carry the reason their JWS twins carry: INVALID_CERTIFICATE. Each receipt is genuine in every other respect, with the signer re-signed by the intermediate wherever the mutation touched its TBS, so the certificate is the only thing a port can object to. The curve case is the one where the signer's KEY is the mutation: the receipt is signed with a real P-256 key whose certificate then names a curve that does not exist, so the port has to refuse the certificate before it can reach the signature — and it must not answer instead that the key is not RSA, which is a different input.

Resource bounds (added 2026-09-05). Every port defends itself against hostile input with size and node budgets, and they sat an order of magnitude apart: a receipt byte cap of 8 MiB in rust, 2 MiB in php, 1 MiB in go and none stated in node, python, java, swift or dotnet; a budget of 200,000 ASN.1 nodes per parse in ruby, 100,000 in rust and go, 20,000 in php and none elsewhere. Those are port-local defences and none of them may quietly become a verdict, so the contract states the floor beneath them rather than the caps themselves. Every implementation MUST accept a well-formed, correctly signed receipt of up to 1 MiB (1,048,576 bytes) of DER whose largest single ASN.1 parse holds up to 20,000 nodes. Those are the two smallest numbers any port already carries — go's byte cap and php's node budget — so the floor raises nothing, and both are an order of magnitude above the largest genuine receipt in the corpus (79 KB, 187 in-app purchases, under 3,000 nodes). Above the floor a port MAY refuse and the number it refuses at is its own business; below it, refusing is a bug. A node is one TLV, counted descending into constructed values only, because a primitive OCTET STRING's contents — an in-app purchase, an attribute value, the encapsulated payload — are a separate parse with a separate budget in every port that has one. Two receipts pin it from below, one number each: `receipt-byte-floor` is 1,034,681 bytes at 9,237 nodes and `receipt-node-floor` is 19,897 nodes at 74,569 bytes. One receipt under both limits would not do it -- a port could lower either cap to just above what that single receipt happened to use, which is what the 809,069-byte, 16,037-node receipt they replace allowed. Neither is also run through verifyReceiptEndpoint: base64 of 1 MB is 1.38 MB, over php's 1 MiB cap on a REQUEST BODY, which bounds a wire request rather than a receipt and is not what this floor is about.

cases.description: The shared generated StoreKit 2 transaction JWS verifies against its own pinned root and decodes to the manifested claims.
A transaction whose bundleId claim is not the configured one is rejected on the claim check, after the signature and chain pass.
A Sandbox transaction offered to a Production-only accept set is rejected (PLAN.md D3: environment routing is an accept-set).
The generated test chain must not verify against the real pinned Apple JWS roots — anchor pinning, not system trust.

With a max signed age configured, a payload signed longer ago than that is rejected as stale — here months before the pinned verification time. The staleness rule is the only verdict in this file that moves with the clock.

The same payload and the same 60-second max age as the stale case, verified 60 seconds after its signedDate: an age exactly equal to the maximum is still fresh. Pins the rule as "older than the maximum", not "at least as old as".

One second later the same payload under the same configuration is stale. This case and the one above differ in nothing but the injected clock, so together they pin the exact boundary of the max-signed-age rule and prove the clock is what decides it.

A clock an hour before the signedDate leaves the payload fresh: age runs from the signing time to now, and a payload from the future is not stale. Catches an implementation that compares the magnitude of the difference instead of its sign.

A JWS leaf lacking marker OID 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1 is rejected even though its chain terminates at the pinned root shipped alongside the fixture (PLAN.md 2.1 step 3). Not exercised by the Java suite today, which asserts the same fact against a run-time generated PKI instead.
A JWS intermediate lacking WWDR marker OID 1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.1 is rejected against its own pinned root. Not exercised by the Java suite today.
Chain validity is judged at the payload signedDate, not at verification time: a 2020-06-01 payload signed by a chain valid 2020-01-01..2021-01-01 still verifies (PLAN.md 2.1 step 4).

The same expired chain signing a 2024-08-06 payload is rejected: the signedDate falls outside the certificate validity window. Deterministic — the window is fixed and already in the past, so no clock is needed.
Apple's own app-store-server-library mock transactionInfo verifies against Apple's vendored test CA — cross-library parity on the exact upstream bytes.
Apple's wrongBundleId mock fixture is rejected on the bundle-id claim check.
Apple's missingX5CHeaderClaim mock fixture is rejected at header parsing: no x5c means no chain to validate (PLAN.md 2.1 step 2).
An Xcode/StoreKit-Test signed transaction carries a single self-signed certificate in x5c; requiring exactly three certificates rejects it before any chain work.
The shared generated Sandbox AppTransaction verifies and decodes to the manifested claims; a Sandbox receiptType needs no appAppleId binding.
An AppTransaction carries no signedDate, so its age is measured from receiptCreationDate (PLAN.md 2.1 step 4). Thirty seconds after that date, under a 60-second max age, it is fresh.
Sixty-one seconds after the same receiptCreationDate the AppTransaction is stale. An implementation that only ever ages a payload by signedDate would find no anchor here and accept it.

A Production AppTransaction whose appAppleId claim matches the configured one verifies. Not exercised by the Java suite against this fixture; Java asserts the same fact against a run-time generated PKI.
In Production the appAppleId claim is binding: a mismatch is rejected (PLAN.md 2.1 step 6).
verifyRaw validates chain and signature but enforces no claim: a verifier configured for a different bundle id still returns the decoded claims unchanged.
Apple's mock renewalInfo has no bundleId claim, so it is only reachable through verifyRaw; chain and signature still hold against Apple's test CA.
Apple's mock App Store Server Notification V2 payload verifies through verifyRaw against Apple's test CA.
The shared generated PKCS#7 receipt verifies, its SHA-1 device hash matches the supplied GUID, and every modelled attribute decodes to the manifested value.
Device binding is enforced when a GUID is supplied: flipping the low bit of the first GUID byte breaks SHA1(guid || opaque || bundleIdBytes) against attribute 5.
A receipt issued for another app is rejected on the bundle-id check, after chain, signer purpose and signature pass.
A byte-identical payload signed by a second, independently generated receipt PKI is rejected against the first PKI root.
Xcode-style receipts wrap the attribute SET in an extra OCTET STRING; parsers must unwrap it rather than reject the receipt.

A signer leaf lacking OID 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1 is rejected even though its chain terminates at the pinned root shipped with the fixture (PLAN.md D13 — closes the developer-certificate forgery hole).
Receipt chain validity is judged at the receipt creation date (attribute 12): a 2020-06-01 receipt signed by a chain valid 2020-01-01..2021-01-01 still verifies (PLAN.md 2.2 step 2).
The same expired receipt chain signing a 2024-08-06 receipt is rejected: the creation date falls outside the certificate validity window. Deterministic — the window is fixed and already in the past.
Attribute types the library does not model are surfaced raw rather than dropped (PLAN.md D10): the shared receipt carries type 9999 with value bytes 01 02 03.
A genuine Apple-signed sandbox receipt on the newer G5 signing chain verifies against the real pinned Apple receipt roots.
A genuine legacy receipt with a full SHA-1 signing chain and 187 in-app purchases verifies against the real pinned Apple receipt roots.

An Xcode-signed receipt carrying real purchases must not verify against the real Apple roots. The configured bundle id is the literal placeholder "*": the chain fails long before any bundle-id comparison.

A genuine Xcode-generated app receipt from Apple's own test data is rejected against the real Apple roots. Chain validation runs before the signer-purpose check, so the reason is INVALID_CHAIN and not INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE (PLAN.md 2.2 step 3).

The verifyReceipt-compatible endpoint answers status 0 for a sandbox receipt on a sandbox instance, rendering numbers as strings and dates as Apple's three-field triple. This case pins no clock, so request_date* is whatever the system clock says and is left unasserted; endpoint/request-date-is-the-verification-clock pins it instead.

request_date is the instant the endpoint answered, so the clock drives it — and drives nothing else: the receipt's own creation date is read from the signed bytes and does not move. The three renderings are Apple's triple: Etc/GMT text, epoch milliseconds as a string, and the same instant in America/Los_Angeles.
A sandbox receipt presented to a production instance routes to 21007 and the response carries neither receipt nor environment.
A receipt that does not chain to the endpoint trust anchors answers 21003 (could not be authenticated), never 21002.
receipt_type "Production" on a production instance answers 0.
receipt_type "Production" on a sandbox instance answers 21008.
receipt_type "ProductionVPP" counts as production (PLAN.md D10 fail-closed routing set).
receipt_type "ProductionVPP" on a sandbox instance answers 21008.
receipt_type "ProductionVPPSandbox" is a sandbox type despite the prefix; on a production instance it answers 21007. The misroute this case pins was found by adversarial review.
receipt_type "ProductionVPPSandbox" on a sandbox instance answers 0.
A receipt with no receipt_type attribute routes as sandbox (fail closed), so a production instance answers 21007.
A receipt with no receipt_type attribute routes as sandbox and answers 0 there.

A receipt attribute whose type INTEGER is 2^31 — one past the largest signed 32-bit value — is rejected as a malformed receipt. The receipt is sound in every other way: trusted chain, valid CMS signature, correct device hash, real bundle id, so the attribute type is the only thing left to object to. Failing closed is the decision: mapping an unrepresentable type onto a sentinel such as -1, or filing it under unknownAttributes under a renamed key, makes two ports disagree about what the same bytes contain.

The same over-range attribute type reaches the endpoint as 21002 (malformed), not 21003: the receipt authenticates fine and it is the payload that cannot be represented. Pins the reason mapping as well as the rejection.

A receipt carrying no attribute 12 verifies: the creation date is optional, and with none to anchor on, certificate validity is judged at current time (PLAN.md 2.2 step 2). This chain is valid until 2050, so the answer is deterministic until then. The companion endpoint cases pin the other half — that "current time" here means the system clock, not an injectable one.

The dateless receipt under a chain that expired in 2021, answered with the clock pinned to 2020-06-01 — inside that chain's validity window. It stays 21003. An injected clock reaches the request_date triple and the max-signed-age rule, never a certificate-validity instant: a caller who injects a clock to test staleness, or to paper over clock skew, must not thereby accept an expired chain. A port that routed the "else current time" fallback through its clock answers 0 here.

The other direction, on a chain valid until 2050: the same dateless receipt answered with the clock pinned to 2099 is still 0. The clock stamps request_date and nothing else, so it can neither authenticate an expired chain nor expire a live one. receipt_creation_date is absent from the body because the receipt states none — the endpoint does not substitute "now" for it.

The JWS half of the same rule. A payload carrying neither signedDate nor receiptCreationDate, signed by a chain that expired in 2021, verified with the clock pinned to 2020-06-01 — inside that window — and a max signed age configured, so the clock does have a legitimate consumer here. It is still INVALID_CHAIN: the staleness rule may read the injected clock, the certificate-validity fallback may not.

A payload that states no signing time cannot be measured against a maximum age, so the max-signed-age rule does not apply: 60 seconds configured and the clock pinned to 2099, and it still verifies. Measuring the clock against itself — treating "now" as the signing time — would make every such payload eternally fresh by accident rather than by rule, and routing the certificate-validity fallback through the same clock would instead make this INVALID_CHAIN, since the chain expires in 2050.

One character of the payload segment was rewritten after the JWS was signed, so the ES256 signature no longer covers the bytes served. Everything a port checks before the signature is deliberately intact: the header is the original one, its three x5c entries parse, leaf and intermediate carry the Apple marker OIDs, the chain validates to the pinned root at the payload's own signedDate, and the payload is still valid base64url JSON naming the configured bundle id and an accepted environment. INVALID_SIGNATURE is therefore the first verdict reachable, and this is the vector that makes every port agree on the answer to "these bytes were altered" — until now each port only asserted it against bytes it mutated at run time, which no shared case could express.

The first x5c entry is base64 of the ASCII text "not a certificate" — well-formed base64 that decodes to bytes no X.509 parser can read. The header was signed in that state, so the signature genuinely covers what is served and the unparseable leaf is the only defect. The verdict is INVALID_CERTIFICATE rather than INVALID_JWS_FORMAT (the entry is present, is a string, and the array still holds exactly three) and rather than INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE (nothing was parsed, so no marker OID could be looked for). The entry chosen is x5c[0] on purpose: Java parses the third entry and the other eight ports never touch it, so a vector built on x5c[2] would pin a divergence instead of a shared rule.

One byte of the receipt's signed payload was flipped after signing, so the CMS content digest no longer matches the one the signature covers. The byte belongs to attribute 9999, which no port models, so the receipt still parses, still carries the configured bundle id, the same creation date and the same opaque value and device hash; the chain still builds to the pinned root at that creation date and the signer still carries the Apple receipt-signing OID. The CMS signature check is the only thing left to fail, which is what makes this a single-fault vector rather than an assertion about check ordering.

A second point on the attribute-type ceiling. receipt/reject-attribute-type-above-int32-max pins 2^31; a port could put its own limit anywhere between there and 2^53 and no vector would notice. This attribute's type is 2^32 + 2, which lands in that band and is chosen rather than picked: truncated to 32 bits it becomes 2, the bundle id attribute, and its value is a well-formed UTF8String reading "com.attacker.app". A port that wrapped instead of rejecting would therefore read a second bundle id out of the receipt and answer WRONG_BUNDLE_ID, so the two verdicts are distinguishable. The receipt is otherwise sound — trusted chain, valid signature, correct bundle id — and INVALID_RECEIPT_FORMAT is the answer for the same reason as at 2^31: fail closed rather than let two ports disagree about what the bytes contain.

Four non-base64url characters are appended to the signature segment of an otherwise genuine, verifying transaction. Everything before the segment decode is intact, so the only question this pins is whether a port decodes a compact-JWS segment strictly. A lenient decoder drops the characters it does not recognise and recovers the original 64 signature bytes, so the payload verifies and the port answers ok; a strict one refuses the segment. This is pinned strict: RFC 7515 section 2 defines the segments as unpadded base64url, and accepting anything else means a port accepts bytes the signature does not cover.

The signature segment of a genuine, verifying transaction is padded to a multiple of four with '='. RFC 7515 section 2 specifies base64url with the padding omitted, so the padded spelling is not a compact JWS. As with the trailing-junk case the decoded signature bytes are unchanged, so a port that tolerates padding answers ok and a port that does not refuses the segment.

The final character of the signature segment is replaced by one that decodes to the same bytes with a different bit pattern in the trailing bits base64url does not use. The decoded signature is byte-identical to the genuine one, so the ES256 check passes wherever the segment decodes at all: this is the same signed transaction under a second spelling. That is what makes it the sharpest of the three. A caller that deduplicates on the JWS string rather than on transactionId (PLAN.md D4) gets a fresh cache key for a payload it has already honoured, so the lenient answer is an accept for every one of the sixteen spellings this substitution admits.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: canonical standard base64, one line: what base64EncodedString(options: []) emits. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: a trailing line feed after the padding. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: wrapped at 64 columns with LF: Foundation's .lineLength64Characters + .endLineWithLineFeed. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: wrapped at 76 columns with CRLF: .lineLength76Characters with the default line ending. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: base64url alphabet with padding: Foundation's .base64URLAlphabet. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: base64url alphabet, padding omitted: .base64URLAlphabet with .omitPaddingCharacters. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: standard alphabet, padding omitted: .omitPaddingCharacters. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: two spaces before and after the text. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: four exclamation marks appended after the padding: no encoder emits them, and a lenient decoder that skips them yields a second spelling of the same receipt. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: four alphabet characters appended after the padding: data after the terminator is not base64. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: one standard-only character replaced by its base64url twin, so both alphabets appear in one string, which no encoder produces. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.
The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: zero bytes. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: one exclamation mark inserted at offset 100. Same DER underneath in every accept case, so the only thing that can move the verdict is the base64 decoder.
The same 05-urlsafe-padded string in receipt-data: the endpoint decodes with the library's rule and answers 0.
The same 09-junk-after-padding string in receipt-data: the endpoint decodes with the library's rule and answers 21002.
The same 12-empty string in receipt-data: the endpoint decodes with the library's rule and answers 21002.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: the genuine string already ends in '==' and two more are appended: a padding run of four, which no RFC 4648 encoder emits. Characters after the padding are refused, and '=' is not exempt -- otherwise padding is a free suffix and the receipt has one spelling per extra '='. Same DER underneath, so only the decoder can move the verdict.

The genuine sandbox receipt as the string a client would send: one of the two required '=' is removed: padding is accepted when omitted entirely and when canonical, never when partial, because no encoder emits a partial run and a decoder that tolerates one is guessing. Same DER underneath, so only the decoder can move the verdict.

The genuine receipt's base64 with its final data character removed and three '=' appended: the data length is 1 mod 4, which no base64 encoding can have, yet the total is a multiple of four. A decoder that checks the length only after counting the padding, or that treats three '=' as a canonical run, accepts an encoding RFC 4648 cannot produce. The unpadded data length must be checked first, and three '=' is never canonical.

The header is `{"alg":"ES256","x5c":[1,2,3]}` and was signed in that state, so the ES256 signature covers exactly the bytes served and the JSON types are the only defect. The array is present and holds exactly three entries, so what fails is the type of each one, before any of them is base64-decoded: INVALID_JWS_FORMAT, the same verdict a header with no x5c at all gets, and not INVALID_CERTIFICATE, which would say something was decoded and found wanting. The statically typed ports get this from decoding the header into an array of strings; the dynamically typed ones have to check it, and Python did not until fuzzing walked a TypeError out of base64.b64decode and past every `except` in the library. A port that reads only the entries it uses would also have to be caught by this vector, which is why all three are numbers rather than just the leaf.

The payload claims `signedDate: 1e300` — about 10^289 years, a valid JSON number that no calendar type can hold. Certificate validity is judged at the payload signing date (PLAN.md 2.1 step 4), and an instant that cannot be expressed is inside no validity window, so the verdict is INVALID_CHAIN. The ports reach it by different routes and must agree on the answer: Node builds an Invalid Date, whose every comparison is false; Python refuses to build the datetime at all and has to turn the OverflowError into this verdict rather than let it escape. NaN and Infinity land in the same place in the ports whose JSON parser accepts them, but most reject both outright, so the vector is the huge-but-valid number rather than a value half the ports cannot even parse.

One byte of x5c[1] is changed: the basicConstraints extnValue OCTET STRING is left claiming 127 content bytes inside an extension that declares 15, so the certificate stops decoding partway through its extension block. Everything before that region is intact and the header was signed in this state. The verdict is INVALID_CERTIFICATE — the entry is present, is a string and decodes from base64, but what comes out is not a certificate all the way down. What this vector pins that `transaction/reject-x5c-leaf-that-is-not-a-certificate` cannot is that a port must PARSE an x5c certificate rather than scan it: the corruption sits past the marker OID a port looks for, so an implementation that walks the DER only far enough to answer "does it carry 1.2.840.113635.100.6.2.1" accepts the whole JWS. It is x5c[1] rather than x5c[0] so that the two certificate vectors cover both entries every port loads.

x5c[1]'s namedCurve is rewritten to 1.2.840.10045.3.1.10, which is unassigned, and its TBS is re-signed by the root so the certificate is genuine in every other respect and a broken issuer signature is not what a port objects to first. A public key cannot be built on a curve the implementation does not have, so the certificate is one this library never understood: INVALID_CERTIFICATE, alongside the other two x5c defects, rather than INVALID_CHAIN. That reading was adopted AGAINST the six-to-three majority the ports arrived with, because the three in the minority (java, swift, go) reject the certificate while decoding it and pinning INVALID_CHAIN would have required them to defer a rejection they already make. It also closes a latent escape in Node, where reading the certificate's public key raises a raw OpenSSL decode error and only the order of the issuer check kept it from reaching a caller. The requirement underneath the reason is that the failure is a verdict at all: an unimplemented curve surfaces as a library-specific exception type — cryptography's UnsupportedAlgorithm was not in Python's except list — and a caller catching the verification error sees a crash instead.

x5c[1] claims X.509 version 11, and its TBS is re-signed by the root so nothing else about it is wrong: the extensions decode, the marker OID is there, the validity window covers the signing date, and it really did issue the leaf. X.509 defines v1, v2 and v3 and nothing else, so the only thing that can reject this input is a version check, which is why a port without one accepts a certificate whose format it does not know. INVALID_CERTIFICATE: the bytes are not a certificate this library can be said to have understood, and the fault is in the certificate rather than in the path it sits on.

x5c[0] carries its basicConstraints extension twice — a byte-identical second copy appended to the extension list — and its TBS is re-signed by the intermediate so the certificate is genuine in every other respect: the marker OID is there, the validity window covers the signing date, the key is the one that signed the JWS, and the intermediate really did issue it. RFC 5280 4.2 says a certificate MUST NOT include more than one instance of a particular extension, and a parser that allows one has to pick a copy, so two ports reading the same bytes can disagree about whether the certificate is a CA, what it may be used for, or whether it carries a marker OID at all. INVALID_CERTIFICATE for the same reason as transaction/reject-x5c-corrupt-extension: the entry is present, is a string, and decodes, but what comes out is not a certificate this library can be said to have read. It is not INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE, which would say the extensions were read and the marker OID was missing. The duplicated extension is basicConstraints rather than the marker OID because it is the one every port reaches: a port that scans for 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1 and never decodes the rest of the block accepts this JWS. It sits on the leaf because that is the certificate whose extensions every port touches first, and Python's fuzzer found it there — cryptography raises DuplicateExtension, which derives from Exception rather than ValueError and so passed every except in the JWS path and reached the caller as a crash.

The THIRD x5c entry is base64 of the ASCII text "not a certificate" — well-formed base64 that decodes to bytes no X.509 parser can read, and the header was signed in that state, so the unparseable third entry is the only defect. It is the index twin of transaction/reject-x5c-leaf-that-is-not-a-certificate, which deliberately sits on x5c[0] because this index was the one differential no shared vector covered: java decoded and parsed all three entries and answered INVALID_CERTIFICATE, while node, python, swift, go, ruby, rust, php and dotnet never touched the third entry and VERIFIED the JWS. Eight ports to one, and the majority was overruled by the rule that settled transaction/reject-x5c-unimplemented-curve: pinning acceptance would have made java drop a rejection it already makes, and no reading of this library lets an input it cannot parse through because the parse was optional. INVALID_CERTIFICATE, the same verdict the other two unreadable-certificate vectors carry. What does NOT change is trust: x5c[2] is still never compared to an anchor and never trusted anywhere, so a well-formed JWS whose third entry an attacker swapped still verifies or fails exactly as before — the entry now has to be a certificate, not the right one.

The payload's signedDate is written `1722945600000.0` — the same instant every other generated transaction states, spelled with a decimal point. JSON draws no line between that and `1722945600000`, so the claim is the same claim and the JWS verifies. This is the boundary of `transaction/reject-signed-date-out-of-range`: a port that answers that vector by refusing every number which is not a bare integer passes it and fails this one, and the failure is in the accept direction — a signedDate read as absent moves certificate validity onto the current-time fallback that PLAN.md 2.1 step 4 reserves for a payload stating no date, and silences the staleness rule with it. The ports read the value rather than its spelling by different routes: node `typeof === 'number'`, java `canConvertToLong()`, python `isinstance(x, (int, float))`, swift `as? Double`, rust and dotnet a bounded float with truncation toward zero, php a bounded `(int)` cast, ruby the Numeric as it stands. Go read the literal (`json.Number.Int64`) and was the one port this vector was written against. signedDate is deliberately NOT pinned in `fields`: what a port returns for a claim spelled this way is its own numeric type, and `transaction/reject-stale-payload-signed-date-decimal` pins that the VALUE was read.

The same decimally-spelled payload under a 60-second max signed age, verified months later: STALE_PAYLOAD. Acceptance alone cannot show that the date was read — this chain is valid at the current time too, so a port ignoring the claim would verify the accept case for the wrong reason. The staleness rule is the observable that only fires when the value reaches it, and it is the control an attacker most wants switched off.

The certificate a legacy PKCS#7 receipt is signed by claims X.509 version 11, and its TBS is re-signed by the intermediate so nothing else about it is wrong. The receipt is genuine in every other respect — the signer really did sign it, the intermediate really did issue the signer, the chain terminates at the root shipped with the fixture, the marker OID is there and the validity window covers the creation date — so the certificate is the only thing a port can object to. X.509 defines v1, v2 and v3 and nothing else, so only a version check can reject this input. INVALID_CERTIFICATE, the reason transaction/reject-x5c-certificate-version-11 pins for the same mutation in a JWS header. It needs its own vector because the version check sat on the JWS path alone in node, python, ruby and dotnet: the four ports that settle what their platform decoder lets past while the verdict is still "this is not a certificate" were settling it for x5c entries only, and the CMS signer went unchecked.

The signer certificate carries its basicConstraints extension twice — a byte-identical second copy appended to the extension list — and its TBS is re-signed by the intermediate. The receipt is genuine in every other respect — the signer really did sign it, the intermediate really did issue the signer, the chain terminates at the root shipped with the fixture, the marker OID is there and the validity window covers the creation date — so the certificate is the only thing a port can object to. RFC 5280 4.2 forbids a second instance of any extension, and a reader that allows one has to pick which copy the certificate means, so the same bytes stop having one answer to "is this a CA", "what may it be used for" and "does it carry the receipt-signing marker OID" — the last of which this path asks. INVALID_CERTIFICATE rather than INVALID_CERTIFICATE_PURPOSE, which would say the extensions were read and the marker OID was missing. The duplicated extension is basicConstraints rather than the marker OID for the same reason as in the JWS twin: it is the one a port reaches even if it only scans for 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1.

The signer's KEY is the mutation. The receipt is signed with a real P-256 key, and the certificate that key sits in then names 1.2.840.10045.3.1.10, which is unassigned, with the TBS re-signed by the intermediate. The receipt is genuine in every other respect — the signer really did sign it, the intermediate really did issue the signer, the chain terminates at the root shipped with the fixture, the marker OID is there and the validity window covers the creation date — so the certificate is the only thing a port can object to. A public key cannot be built on a curve the implementation does not have, so the signature this receipt carries can never be checked — and the port must say so as a verdict about the certificate, before it reaches the signature at all. INVALID_CERTIFICATE, as transaction/reject-x5c-unimplemented-curve pins, and specifically NOT the verdict a port reaches by noticing that the key is not RSA: a readable non-RSA signer key is a different input with a different answer, and this one is a certificate the library never understood. The requirement underneath the reason is that the failure is a verdict at all — an unimplemented curve surfaces as a library-specific exception type, and a caller catching the verification error otherwise sees a crash.

One byte of the signer certificate is changed, and it is one byte further in than the JWS twin changes. transaction/reject-x5c-corrupt-extension rewrites the extnValue OCTET STRING's own length, which breaks the DER of everything that contains it — harmless in a JWS header, where the certificate is a base64 string of its own, and wrong inside a CMS, where it would break the receipt's DER and make every port that walks the whole blob answer about the receipt instead of about the certificate. So the corruption sits INSIDE the OCTET STRING: the BasicConstraints SEQUENCE it holds is left claiming 127 content bytes in a two-byte value. A reader walking generic ASN.1 sees a well-formed primitive of the length it declares and never looks in, so the receipt parses, the chain validates, the payload is intact and the CMS signature is real; only a reader that DECODES the signer's extension block finds the defect, and that is precisely what this vector observes. The certificate has no TBS left to re-sign and no verifier can reach its signature to notice. INVALID_CERTIFICATE: the signer is embedded and is the certificate the SignerInfo names, but what comes out is not a certificate all the way down. The corruption sits past the marker OID a port looks for, so an implementation that walks the DER only far enough to answer "does it carry 1.2.840.113635.100.6.11.1" accepts the whole receipt.

The byte half of the normative resource floor: a well-formed, correctly signed receipt of 1,034,681 bytes of DER — 98.7% of the 1,048,576 the contract promises — which every port MUST accept. Its payload attribute set holds 9,237 nodes, under half the node budget, so what accepting it says is about bytes and nothing else; receipt/verify-at-the-node-floor pins the other number the same way round. Two receipts rather than one because a single fixture under both limits lets a port lower either cap to just above what that one fixture happens to use — the receipt this pair replaces was 809,069 bytes and 16,037 nodes, and a port capping at 900,000 bytes or 17,000 nodes passed it. The size is 2,300 in-app purchases and nothing else: no padding attribute and no inflated wrapper, only product ids padded to 262 characters, which sit in the value of a MODELLED attribute a port must decode and return. The fields pin the collection so a port cannot pass by truncating it, and the first and last purchases keep short product ids so a case can select them by one. Deliberately not also run through verifyReceiptEndpoint: base64 of 1 MB is 1.38 MB, over php's 1 MiB cap on a REQUEST BODY, which bounds a wire request rather than a receipt and is not what this floor is about.

The node half of the normative resource floor: a well-formed, correctly signed receipt whose payload attribute set is one parse of 19,897 nodes — 99.5% of the 20,000 the contract promises — which every port MUST accept. It is 74,569 bytes, a fourteenth of the byte floor, so what accepting it says is about the node budget alone. Ten in-app purchases carry the receipt's real shape; the node count comes from 4,955 further attributes of three bytes each whose types this library does not model. That is the honest shape for this number rather than a shortcut: a node budget is spent per TLV walked, whatever the TLV means, and an unmodelled attribute is walked, counted and recorded under unknownAttributes like any other — the fields below pin two of them, at each end of the run, so a port cannot pass by skipping what it does not recognise. Building the same node count out of in-app purchases would have cost a megabyte of repository for a fixture whose whole subject is the count.
